World.title: From C5 to C6: how Azerbaijan is reshaping balance of power in Central Asia
World.content:
Azerbaijan at Central Asia’s table

On 16 November 2025, the five Central Asian states accepted Azerbaijan as a full member of the Consultative Meeting of Heads of State. Eight months later, on 31 July, Ilham Aliyev took his place at the table at an informal summit in Cholpon-Ata not as a guest, but as one of six equal participants.

The format is now officially known as “Central Asia and Azerbaijan”. The term “C6” has already entered expert vocabulary and is being used at conferences.

The change expands Central Asia’s political and economic cooperation to the western shore of the Caspian Sea. It also turns Azerbaijan from an external partner into a full participant in a route connecting the region with Turkey and Europe.

How did the format emerge and why has it expanded?

Uzbek President Shavkat Mirziyoyev proposed the idea of a consultative mechanism at the UN in September 2017. The first meeting took place in Astana on 15 March 2018. The format’s advantage was its simplicity: without a treaty, permanent secretariat or supranational bodies, the leaders of the five countries could directly discuss borders, water resources, trade and security.

Azerbaijan did not join the process immediately. Ilham Aliyev attended meetings in Dushanbe in 2023, Astana in 2024 and Tashkent in 2025 as an honorary guest. Since the beginning of 2023, he has visited Central Asian countries 16 times, while the region’s leaders have travelled to Azerbaijan 26 times. In 2025, Azerbaijan’s trade with the five Central Asian states grew by 53% to $1.8 billion. Trade among the Central Asian countries themselves reached $10.7 billion in 2024.

Mirziyoyev described Baku’s accession as an opportunity to create a “single space for cooperation” between Central Asia and the South Caucasus. Aliyev, in turn, described the two shores of the Caspian as a “single geopolitical and geoeconomic space”.

The leaders of Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, Tajikistan and Turkmenistan said they supported expanding the format because it would create new opportunities for transit, logistics and energy cooperation.

The Middle Corridor and the Caspian’s role in bringing the region together

The geography offers the clearest explanation for Azerbaijan’s participation in the format. The Middle Corridor links China and Central Asia with Europe: goods travel by rail across Kazakhstan to the ports of Aktau and Kuryk, then across the Caspian Sea to Alat, before continuing through Georgia towards Turkey and the Black Sea. Azerbaijan effectively serves as the western gateway to the route.

According to the Kazakh government, freight volumes along the Trans-Caspian route rose by 62% in 2024 to 4.5 million tonnes. Baku says the volume of cargo travelling through the Azerbaijani section of the Middle Corridor has increased by 90% over three years. The authorities plan to raise the capacity of the Port of Alat to 25 million tonnes a year. The World Bank estimates that if countries coordinate border procedures, tariffs, port operations and transport schedules, freight volumes along the corridor could triple by 2030, while delivery times could fall by half.

The plans go beyond container shipping. Proposed electricity and digital cable projects across the Caspian would also bring energy and information flows into the broader agenda of regional cooperation.

The route through Nakhchivan offers new opportunities but remains contentious. The Washington Declaration, signed on 8 August 2025, provides for a transport link through Armenia between mainland Azerbaijan and Nakhchivan, based on the sovereignty and jurisdiction of the states concerned, as well as the development of the TRIPP mechanism. Baku calls the route the “Zangezur Corridor”.

If implemented, the route could give the Middle Corridor an additional link to Turkey. However, until the parties agree on customs procedures, security arrangements, financing and management mechanisms, it remains a project rather than an operational transport corridor.

What is changing from a geopolitical perspective?

“C6” is a convenient political label, not the official name of an organisation. The format remains a consultative platform based on consensus. It does not involve collective defence commitments or mechanisms to enforce decisions.

For Moscow, this is therefore primarily about competition over logistics and political influence, including through the development of routes that bypass Russia, rather than the emergence of a new military alliance.

Beijing gains an additional route to the west and more stable conditions for transit.

Ankara has an interest in strengthening direct transport links across the Caspian.

The European Union and the US see the format as an opportunity to reduce dependence on routes through Russia and expand access to Central Asia.

The new C6 format should not be confused with the Organisation of Turkic States. The OTS has a treaty-based framework and institutional cooperation among Turkic states. The “Central Asia and Azerbaijan” format also includes Tajikistan and focuses less on shared identity than on geography, economic interests and regional cooperation.

Potential opportunities and real constraints

The potential areas for cooperation are quite concrete: common transit tariffs, digital customs procedures, coordinated port and railway schedules, joint investment funds, green energy exports, tourism routes and coordination at international forums. With its ports, financial resources and transport links through the Caucasus and Turkey, Azerbaijan offers Central Asian countries additional routes and opportunities. Baku, in turn, gains more systematic access to the region’s five markets and their economic ties with China.

However, there are also many constraints. The six countries differ in their economic potential, interests in water resources and energy, and priorities in their relations with Russia, China, Turkey and the West. The format has no permanent secretariat or mechanisms to enforce decisions, so implementation of political agreements will depend on intergovernmental coordination.

The Convention on the Legal Status of the Caspian Sea, signed in 2018, has yet to be ratified by Iran, while delimiting the seabed requires separate agreements. Falling water levels in the Caspian, the shallowing of ports and the need for costly dredging also increase the environmental and economic costs of transport logistics.

From symbol to concrete projects?

Mirziyoyev has already proposed transforming the format into a “Community of Central Asia” with a rotating secretariat. The next official meeting, scheduled for 8 October 2026 in Avaza, will be one of the first tests of whether these intentions can turn into practical decisions.

Will the six countries agree on common tariffs, digital customs procedures and a stable ferry schedule? Will TRIPP become a fully fledged part of the Middle Corridor without creating new border disputes? Or will the “Central Asia and Azerbaijan” format remain a flexible consultative platform, with its informal nature continuing to be its main advantage?

Azerbaijan at Central Asia’s table

World.title: Convicted former Georgian PM Garibashvili: ‘Authorities left me no choice, I have to fight’
World.content:
Letter from Georgia’s former prime minister from prison

Convicted former Georgian prime minister Irakli Garibashvili says in a letter published from prison that the authorities arrested him to end his political career. He also says he gave up his legal fight to avoid a confrontation with the authorities.

The former prime minister writes that he received a letter from Regional Development Minister Mamuka Mdinaradze in July. According to Garibashvili, he confirmed to Mdinaradze that same day that he did not intend to return to politics.

Mamuka Mdinaradze’s press office has described Garibashvili’s claims as “complete absurdity”.

“I state with full responsibility that I did everything to avoid confrontation with the [ruling] team and with someone who is dear to me,” Garibashvili wrote.

He says this is why he abandoned his legal challenge and went through the entire process to the end — to avoid, as he put it, harming the interests of the state and the “team”.

“Unfortunately, in response I received a staged dirty provocation, a sea of lies and injustice. Throughout this time, the public heard not a single word from me. I endured this ordeal patiently,” Garibashvili said.

According to Garibashvili, despite the position he had expressed to Mdinaradze, the authorities believed there was still a “1% risk” that he might return to politics in the future.

“To avoid this, they wanted me to face corruption charges and admit guilt,” Garibashvili writes.

According to him, this demand became a “red line” that forced him to take the “most difficult step of my life” — to turn against the authorities.

“I have no other choice. I am forced to start fighting,” the former prime minister said.

On 17 August 2026, Garibashvili made his first public statement from prison. In a Facebook post, he said he had received an ultimatum in a letter sent on the instructions of Bidzina Ivanishvili. He added that he had “no other choice” but to stand against what he described as “evil that insults my dignity”.

“I tried to do everything possible to avoid taking this step, but unfortunately I have no other choice but to confront this evil that insults my dignity. I must confront this ruthless cruelty, oppression and injustice, as well as the dirty plan to destroy me and my family,” Garibashvili wrote.

He also said that Bidzina Ivanishvili and the government bear responsibility for the safety of both himself and his family.

In the letter, Garibashvili says he had remained publicly silent and patiently endured what was happening until now. However, he says the current situation has left him no choice but to begin fighting.

Letter from Georgia’s former prime minister from prison

World.title: Uzbekistan's trade services reach $14.3 bln in 1H 2026
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, August 21. Uzbekistan's trade services turnover reached nearly 170 trillion soums ($14.3 billion) in January-June 2026, increasing 14.9% compared with the same period last year.

This was reflected in the statement by the National Statistics Committee of Uzbekistan.

Tashkent city accounted for the largest volume of trade services at 71.8 trillion soums ($6 billion), followed by Tashkent region at 14.8 trillion soums ($1.2 billion), Fergana region at 12.1 trillion soums ($1 billion) and Samarkand region at 11.3 trillion soums ($950.7 million).

Namangan and Andijan regions each recorded 9.1 trillion soums ($766 million) in trade services, while Bukhara region reached 7.4 trillion soums ($622.6 million) and Kashkadarya region 7 trillion soums ($589 million).

Surkhandarya region accounted for 6.5 trillion soums ($547 million), followed by Khorezm region at 5.2 trillion soums ($437.4 million) and the Republic of Karakalpakstan at 4.8 trillion soums ($404 million).

Jizzakh and Navoi regions each recorded 4 trillion soums ($336.5 million), while Syrdarya region posted the lowest volume at 2.6 trillion soums ($219 million).

Trend's analysis shows that trade services in Uzbekistan remain heavily concentrated in Tashkent, which alone generated around 42.2% of the country's total trade services turnover during the first half of 2026. The capital's volume was almost five times higher than that of Tashkent region, which ranked second.

Trend's calculations show that Tashkent city and Tashkent region together accounted for 86.6 trillion soums (about $7.2 billion), or approximately 50.9% of the country's total trade services turnover. The top four locations — Tashkent city, Tashkent region, Fergana and Samarkand — generated around 110 trillion soums (around $9.2 billion), equivalent to nearly 64.7% of the national total.

The concentration is even more pronounced when compared with lower-performing regions. Tashkent city's trade services turnover was about 27.6 times higher than Syrdarya's 2.6 trillion soums (approx. $218.7 million).

The figures also come against continued expansion of Uzbekistan's broader services economy. Total market services reached 664.9 trillion soums (about $56 billion) in January-June 2026, up 16.9% year on year, with trade services remaining the largest individual segment at 170 trillion soums (around $14.3 billion).

Trade services accounted for approximately 25.6% of all market services in the first half of 2026, making the segment a major contributor to the country's rapidly expanding services economy. Trade, accommodation and food services, financial services and transport together generated 493.3 trillion soums (about $41.5 billion), or about 74% of total market services during the period.

Trend's assessment show that the strong concentration of trade services in Tashkent reflects the capital's role as Uzbekistan's primary commercial and consumer market. At the same time, the substantial gap between Tashkent and most regions indicates that the expansion of trade-related services remains uneven geographically. Further growth outside the capital could therefore provide an additional source of regional economic activity as Uzbekistan's services sector continues to expand.

World.title: Child treated for tuberculosis attended Tasmanian daycare centre
World.content:
A childcare centre in Tasmania's north has confirmed a child who has been treated for the infectious bacterial disease tuberculosis attended the centre.

The child, whose age and gender have not been disclosed for confidentiality reasons, last attended the Kings Meadow Goodstart Early Learning Centre in mid-July.

The centre caters for children aged between six months and six years old.

A spokesperson from Goodstart said the centre was first informed of the case last week and began contacting families of children at the centre yesterday.

Close contacts of the child, including children and staff, have been offered precautionary testing, which is being coordinated by Tasmania's Department of Health and the Launceston General Hospital.

The ABC understands the risk of transmission is low and this is an isolated case.

"The centre remains open and continues to operate as normal with the rigorous hygiene and cleaning part of our usual routine," the spokesperson said.

The centre continues to operate as normal with "rigorous hygiene and cleaning part of our usual routine", the operator says. (ABC News: Kelsey Reid)

Tuberculosis is relatively rare in Australia, and while it can be deadly if left untreated, it can be treated with antibiotics.

The Australian Centre for Disease Control says tuberculosis causes an estimated 1.3 million deaths worldwide annually.

Countries with a high prevalence of TB include India, Indonesia, Philippines, Pakistan and Vietnam, according to the World Health Organization.

The spokesperson from Goodstart said their response had been coordinated with state authorities in alignment with their own policies.

"We've closely followed the directions of Public Health Tasmania and our own infectious diseases policy since being contacted last week," they said.

" Families with concerns are being asked to directly contact their GP or the Public Health Hotline on 1800 671 738. "

The spokesperson also said the child had attended another childcare centre in the area.

Tasmania's Department of Health lists suspected tuberculosis as an urgent category 1 medical condition requiring urgent assessment.

The Australian Centre for Disease Control website states that tuberculosis vaccinations are only recommended for Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander children aged under five, some healthcare workers and children born to parents from countries with high tuberculosis incidence or those travelling to countries with high instances of the disease.

The Tasmanian Health Department has been contacted for comment.

World.title: AFP charges Russian Australian man with foreign interference offence
World.content:
The Australian Federal Police (AFP) has charged a Russian Australian man with foreign interference.

The 27-year-old was arrested yesterday in Sumner, in Brisbane's west, but the AFP says he is a "Victorian resident".

He has been charged with attempting to engage in intentional foreign interference and will appear in the Brisbane Magistrates Court today.

Police are expected to provide more details later today at a press conference in Canberra.

Alleged Russian spies charged with new offence Crown prosecutors presented a new bench charge for the couple of conspiracy to commit espionage.

It is not the first time that police have accused Russia of orchestrating foreign interference in Australia.

Australia has been one of Ukraine's most prominent supporters following Russia's invasion and has funnelled about $1.8 billion to the country in military, economic and humanitarian support over the last four years.

That seems to have coincided with a campaign of Russian espionage in Australia.

In 2024, two Russian-born Australian citizens, married couple Kira and Igor Korolev, were arrested and accused of allegedly attempting to gather and send state secrets to Russia.

Russian hackers warning The hackers are targeting systems in defence, energy and communication sectors.

In June, the charges against them were upgraded to conspiracy to commit espionage.

ASIO director Mike Burgess said his agency had forced out a "hive of spies" from an unnamed country in 2022. They were said to be trying to covertly recruit Australians and steal sensitive information.

Multiple media outlets later reported that Russia was the country running that network, although ASIO has never publicly confirmed this.

Last month, the Australian Signals Directorate (ASD) and nearly two dozen partner agencies issued a joint warning accusing Russian-linked hackers of targeting critical Australian industries, including defence, communications, energy and financial services.

In 2018, the Turnbull government announced it was expelling two Russian diplomats, who it said were undeclared intelligence operatives, as part of global action against Moscow over an alleged nerve agent attack on a former Russian spy living in the UK.

This year, authorities also charged three Chinese nationals with trying to gather intelligence on a Canberra Buddhist group for Chinese security agencies.

World.title: Hong Kong Tiananmen vigil organisers convicted
World.content:
Two former organisers of Hong Kong's decades-old vigil in remembrance of the 1989 Tiananmen Square crackdown have been convicted of incitement to subversion.

The decision was handed down on Friday, local time, in a national security case brought under a China-imposed law that has effectively crushed the city's previously thriving pro-democracy movement.

Lee Cheuk-yan and Chow Hang-tung, former leaders of the Hong Kong Alliance in Support of Patriotic Democratic Movements of China, were charged in 2021 with inciting subversion under the national security law.

Tiananmen Square candlelight vigil trial Lee Cheuk-yan and Chow Hang-tung face up to 10 years in jail if convicted of "incitement to subversion". Advocates say the trial is part of a crackdown by Beijing on long-enjoyed freedoms in Hong Kong.

They both pleaded not guilty and now face a maximum prison term of 10 years. The alliance was also found guilty.

For three decades, the city's candlelight vigil, organised by the alliance, was the only large-scale public commemoration in China of the Tiananmen Square massacre and regularly drew tens of thousands of people annually to mourn the victims.

The event was banned in 2020 during the first year of the COVID-19 pandemic, weeks before Beijing imposed its security law on Hong Kong to quell the 2019 massive anti-government protests.

Observers said their trial symbolises the erosion of freedom of expression in the former British colony, which returned to Chinese rule in 1997.

They are expected to be sentenced at a later date.

Organisers accused of inciting the overthrow of China's ruling party

During the trial, prosecutors said the case was not political and focused on what they viewed as a call by the alliance to incite others to overthrow the leadership of China's ruling Communist Party through unlawful means, pointing to "ending one-party rule", one of the group's core demands.

But Lee told the court that the call was not about ending the party's leadership but about moving toward democracy, letting the people decide who leads them, and that the Communist Party should not enforce "dictatorship".

Tens of thousands of people at a candlelight vigil at Hong Kong's Victoria Park on June 4, 2014, to mark the 25th anniversary of the Tiananmen Square massacre. (Reuters/Bobby Yip)

Chow, a barrister who defended herself, said "ending one-party rule" meant ending a state where power was unrestricted. She criticised how the standard for determining right and wrong was turned upside down in this case.

In a Patreon post on Thursday, she recalled being shackled in handcuffs, and in waist and ankle chains, for trips to court from prison, saying she was walked by correctional service officers "like a dog".

"Justice lives in the hearts of the people. There is no need to look up to this kind of top-down ruling, and one verdict doesn't matter much," she said.

The trial, initially scheduled for 75 days, moved faster than expected and concluded its closing statements on the 24th day.

When it began in January, Albert Ho, another defendant in the case, entered a guilty plea in a move that typically could result in a reduced sentence.

Lee and Chow are expected to plead for lesser penalties at a separate hearing and could be sentenced at a later date alongside Ho.

Supporters cast doubt on allegations

Dozens of people lined up outside the court under drizzling rain ahead of the hearing.

Tang Ngok-kwan, a former alliance member, said police would not let him join the line if he brought "sensitive" materials, including bookmarks printed with "vindicate June 4" — the date of the Tiananmen Square crackdown.

He decided not to go into court.

Former vigil-goer Margaret Chan, who joined the queue at 6am, said the alliance's name carried the word "patriotic".

"Everyone is patriotic. How to incite? Incite others to be patriotic?" she said.

Over seven weeks in 1989, students led peaceful pro-democracy protests centred on Beijing's Tiananmen Square. (AP: Sadayuki Mikami) (AP: Sadayuki Mikami)

Hundreds of people, and possibly thousands, were killed in the 1989 crackdown as military tanks rolled into the centre of Beijing.

It was a pivotal moment in China's modern history, determining that the market reforms that transformed the country into the world's second-largest economy would not be coupled with political liberalisation.

After COVID-19 restrictions were lifted, the former vigil site in Hong Kong was occupied instead each June 4 by a carnival and market stalls organised by pro-Beijing groups.

Beijing said the 2020 security law was necessary for the city's stability.

Many leading activists have been jailed under the same law, including pro-democracy former media tycoon Jimmy Lai.

Under the drastic political changes, dozens of civil society groups also dissolved, including the alliance.

AP

World.title: Panthers NRL finals charge dealt blow by Cogger's three-match ban
World.content:
Penrith is in for a NRL finals selection dilemma after key addition Jack Cogger received a three-match ban for his high shot on Tyran Wishart.

Just when the streaky Panthers looked to have found their best option at five-eighth, Cogger received a grade-two charge that rules him out until after the first week of finals.

Unless Cogger can plead his case at the judiciary and win, the Panthers will be forced to recall out-of-favour Blaize Talagi or Perth-bound Jack Cole.

Storm's finals dream over as Penrith holds on despite triple sin-binning The Penrith Panthers hold on to beat the Melbourne Storm 22-14 and end their faint mathematical hopes of making the NRL finals.

Cogger was sent to the sin bin after rushing out of the line to hit Wishart late in the Panthers' 22-14 win on Thursday night.

He has already been suspended once this season for a similar shot, missing two weeks on that occasion for rushing out and hitting South Sydney's Ashton Ward.

If he unsuccessfully challenges his charge at the judiciary, Cogger will miss an additional game, potentially ruling him out for the remainder of the season.

Cogger also received a $3,000 fine for a shot on Storm forward Angus Hinchey earlier in the clash.

But the 29-year-old's suspension is a far bigger blow for a Penrith side fighting to lock up a top-two finish.

Cogger has been a valuable addition to the Panthers' starting side in recent weeks, proving a more assured defensive presence than Talagi.

His ball-playing has also helped take pressure off halfback Nathan Cleary, as it did during Penrith's comeback victory in the 2023 grand final.

But Cogger's illegal tackle has now opened the door for either Talagi or Cole, one of whom is set to start in the halves for next week's clash with Canterbury.

AAP

World.title: Is super a bigger political bomb than Medicare? We're about to find out
World.content:
Barnaby Joyce had just said "lie" for the 17th time when the line went dead.

A few moments later, dialled back into his Radio National interview, he joked listeners had missed him in "full flight" about Jim Chalmers's claim One Nation and the Coalition were "against universal super". It was, he said, a lie to rival the infamous "Mediscare".

It's a telling comparison. Joyce fought the 2016 election when Bill Shorten's Labor ran the brutally effective scare campaign that the Coalition planned to privatise Medicare.

And Chalmers, invigorated by comments about super from Pauline Hanson and Liberal Andrew Bragg, has wasted no time in framing the next election as a super "referendum", spamming social media with claims his opponents want to "destroy" the system.

That's a bit much. Hanson only said super should be "lightened up a bit", perhaps by letting people access more of their funds pre-retirement. Bragg was more colourful, calling compulsory super "a loss of liberty", but his colleagues ran a mile from him.

Still, the line isn't totally fanciful either. One Nation has flagged more policies to come, and there is genuine hostility to super among Coalition MPs, several of whom told the ABC this week they did want to carve out a point of difference with Labor on the subject.

Some within Labor are salivating at that prospect. Asked whether super was as much of a vote-winner as Medicare, a senior Labor figure jubilantly declared: "It's bigger."

But on the right, some believe that voters weighed down by economic gloom will be tempted by the thought that super is their money and they should access it now, not later. So would a super referendum deliver the resounding Yes vote Labor expects?

Labor ran a campaign in the 2016 election accusing the Coalition of a secret plan to privatise Medicare. (Dan Peled: AAP)

Supercharged retirement

Since it began in 1992, compulsory super has substantially boosted the wealth with which Australians retire. That's even before the system is "fully mature" — that is, when retirees have had super for their whole working lives, a milestone still years away.

Super's logic is neat: require people to save some money for their own retirement, give everybody access to the power of compound returns on long-term investments, and reduce the need for pension payments. Labor hails it as "the envy of the world".

But the fact remains that putting money away for tomorrow means less money today. In a legal sense, the amount employers must pay into their workers' super — currently 12 per cent of their wages — is on top of their wages, not instead of them.

But for businesses, the dollar is still a dollar, and a 2020 Grattan Institute report based on a study of enterprise agreements found super increases had come at the expense of wage increases most of the time.

This is contentious terrain, and that finding landed in the middle of a political debate about whether the compulsory amount should increase from 9.5 per cent to 12 per cent. The Coalition resisted, but Labor delivered it in government.

Labor politicians strenuously resist the idea that workers must choose between more super and more wages. But a hint at what they really think is that they have no plans to move to a 15 per cent guarantee, Paul Keating's original vision.

Paul Keating introduced the Superannuation Guarantee in 1992. (Getty/Impressions)

Comparing the pair

At the same time, Treasury and Grattan have warned in recent years that super may be over-preparing people for retirement, such that retirees spend very little of their super before they die or even increase their wealth, passing on large inheritances.

A Treasury retirement income review in 2021 studied the accounts managed by one large super fund and found that members died with 90 per cent of the super they had retired with on average.

Ironically, Labor itself has used this argument when it has proposed less generous tax treatment for those with very high super balances — and the Coalition has usually been on the opposite side of that debate.

But when it comes to the super guarantee, the roles are reversed, and the Treasury finding of 2021 informed a view among many on the conservative side that the guarantee was too high.

Some would even like to wind back the clock, lowering the guarantee to perhaps 10 per cent. Several Liberal politicians told the ABC this had been discussed internally but was viewed as a risky proposition and had slim prospects of becoming opposition policy.

That would truly make the election a referendum on super. The idea could have political appeal if it was presented to voters as a wage rise. But there would be no guarantee that businesses would pass the savings on and, if they did, it would be an inflation risk.

'Depriving my future self': would-be buyers weigh up super withdrawal With home ownership more out of reach than ever for younger Australians, some are pondering whether their retirement fund would be better off used now, to buy a house.

Instead, the Coalition has gone to the last two elections campaigning to erode super a different way; by letting first homebuyers tap their super for a home deposit, an idea spearheaded by Bragg and now-shadow treasurer Tim Wilson.

It's not clear this has been a major factor in either election, for good or ill, but it is hated by economists who say it will push up house prices and will not solve the crisis.

That may even be a design feature. Liberals claim those who drain their super would be no worse off because their money would make a similar return once invested in their home. But that's only true if house prices keep growing above inflation forever.

When do we want it? Now

The Coalition's plans for that policy are ambiguous. But Hanson is now swimming in the same waters. Her policy, which does not exist yet beyond some vague statements, is to allow people to draw down on their super as a cost-of-living measure.

Can you access your super savings before retirement? Should you tap into your super early? There is a trade-off between instant cash and future growth.

Here, unlike the super housing policy, the money withdrawn would likely be spent, not invested. An academic study of the Morrison government's pandemic policy to let some people access $20,000 of their super found gambling was a major spending category.

The line of "gambling with your future" almost writes itself, and One Nation would open itself to a fierce campaign from Labor and a well-endowed super industry which has spent decades building public support for super as the bedrock of financial security.

A war of slogans would follow: "It's your money" up against "It's your future".

Loading

Indicators of future performance

For either One Nation or the Coalition to win that campaign, it would likely need to find some way to discredit those high reserves of public affinity for super. Bragg has been trying this in his own way for years with his claims of "corruption", with little success.

But a sleeper issue on the government's agenda could change this: an overhaul of the "performance test", the rules governing how super funds can invest members' money, a dry and technical process led by assistant treasurer Daniel Mulino.

The industry says the current benchmarks are too restrictive, forcing them into safe bets and inhibiting them from investing in startups or innovation. Funds are so constrained that they have effectively run out of Australian investments and are hunting abroad.

How super could help fund renewables Australian super funds manage $4.5 trillion in retirement savings, but directing some of that war chest towards the clean energy transition could be more difficult than it seems.

Labor has signalled it will broaden the criteria without compromising the requirement for funds to make responsible investments and solid returns. But it is also planning to set "national priorities", such as investment in housing and renewables.

That is a red rag to a bull for conservative super sceptics, and the Coalition has been watching warily for some time. But this week, it was Hanson who blew it up.

"Jim Chalmers cannot stop spending, and now he has his eyes on Australians' superannuation to fund more of Labor's bad ideas," she said in a social media post this week. "Your super is not Labor's piggy bank … Jim Chalmers should keep his hands off."

Loading Instagram content

There is no more truth in the idea that the super performance test changes are a Labor raid on superannuants than there is to Chalmers's claims about his opponents "destroying" super — fighting liar with liar, to use Joyce's word. But it's a reminder that a super war could damage both sides.

Former treasurer Wayne Swan, who now heads a large super fund, acknowledged the risks but said it was a fight Labor was right to pick and should be confident of winning.

"The thing is, it's a cheap trick, a mirage," he told the ABC. "You're telling people you're giving them something when you're just taking it away."

World.title: Fourth Sydney Airport safety incident in three weeks under investigation
World.content:
A fourth incident involving aircraft on the ground at Sydney Airport in just over three weeks is being investigated.

Airservices Australia, the government-owned organisation responsible for air traffic management, said it reported the "potential traffic conflict" between two Qantas planes to safety authorities on Tuesday.

The Australian Transport Safety Bureau (ATSB) said that just after 8am, Qantas flight QF589 had been heading west along taxiway Lima after landing from the Gold Coast.

At the same time, Qantas flight QF405 to Melbourne had been given permission to turn onto that taxiway.

The ATSB said that when the crew of the Melbourne-bound flight noticed the other plane, they stopped and allowed it to pass ahead of them.

"There was no immediate risk of collision, with [QF405] braking normally before coming to a stop," a spokesperson said.

"As such the ATSB has classified this as a safety "incident", rather than a "serious incident", but has elected to conduct an investigation to understand the potential conflicting instructions to the flight crews."

Qantas said its aircraft had been cleared to proceed following instructions from air traffic control.

The airline also said it would support the ATSB's investigation.

Fourth incident

Airservices Australia says each incident is being investigated on its individual facts. (ABC News: John Gunn)

It is the fourth time conflicting instructions have been relayed to planes on Sydney Airport's tarmac in just over three weeks.

On July 27, a Qantas 737 was cleared to cross the main runway, where a QantasLink flight had been landing.

A Jetstar cabin crew member was injured two weeks later, when the plane they were in was forced to slam on its brakes to avoid hitting a Boeing 777 under tow.

Later that same day, a Virgin flight was cleared to take-off before that permission was swiftly rescinded because a Qantas plane had been cleared to cross the same runway more than 1,200 metres in front.

Retired airline pilot says Sydney Airport safety incident 'diminished' Sydney Airport could face "catastrophic" consequences if safety issues are not addressed, a former pilot and aviation safety investigator says.

Each of those incidents are being investigated by the ATSB, which said it would examine whether they had any common contributing factors.

Airservices Australia said all the incidents involved a "range of circumstances".

"Each incident is being investigated on its individual facts," a spokesperson said in a statement.

"Airservices will continue to review operational events and take any action required to maintain safe operations."

World.title: Women in Swans scandal suffering 'severe stress and anxiety', lawyer says
World.content:
A lawyer representing two of the women involved in an alleged sexual assault scandal engulfing the Sydney Swans says his clients are suffering "severe stress and anxiety".

Several adult entertainers are understood to have joined players at Melbourne's Pullman Hotel after being hired in the hours after the Swans' win against Essendon on Sunday night.

Five players — Isaac Heeney, Nick Blakey, Chad Warner, Riley Bice and James Jordon — have been stood down by the Swans for breaching the club's standards on drinking and staying out late following last Sunday's win over Essendon in Melbourne.

Separately, police are investigating a report of sexual assault, which the ABC understands centres on a player allegedly touching one of the women without her consent.

Police have not made any arrests or laid charges.

Lawyer John Karantzis is representing two of the women, who he said would be claiming damages for "pain and suffering" following the incident.

"They're suffering severe stress and anxiety as a result of the events occurring on Monday morning," Mr Karantzis said.

" My clients are suffering severe trauma from what happened. "

Five Sydney Swans players were sanctioned by the club for breaching club standards. (Getty Images: Darrian Traynor)

Mr Karantzis said the women were told the men were carpenters and allege there were more people in the room than the five players identified by the Swans.

The Swans issued a statement rejecting suggestions other people involved with the club were in the room.

"The Sydney Swans can confirm that all investigations carried out by the Club have consistently indicated that the only representatives of the Club in the room central to the police investigation were the five players who have been stood down," the statement said.

"We have every reason to consider that reports to the contrary are simply false."

Mr Karantzis said the women made a complaint to police on Monday morning and were interviewed by police.

He said the women were being supported.

"Fortunately, they've got loving family and we've provided them with professional support which is needed," he said.

Late on Wednesday night, the players who have been stood down issued an apology to everyone involved in the scandal.

This morning Swans Captain Callum Mills said he was "deeply shocked and disappointed" and said he had not witnessed anything like this behaviour before.

"We really are disappointed at the action of these five players," he said.

World.title: Young Docker set for AFL debut as Freo rest three for Blues clash
World.content:
NationalWAAFL 2026 Young Docker set for AFL debut as Freo rest three for Blues clash Justin Chadwick August 21, 2026 — 1:42pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Fremantle coach Justin Longmuir has welcomed Josh Fraser to his special ruck club, praising the new Carlton coach for the way he’s turned around the Blues’ fortunes. Carlton were a rabble at 1-8 when Fraser inherited the coaching reins on an interim basis following Michael Voss’ decision to step down. Tobyn Murray is set to make his AFL debut when Fremantle take on Carlton on Saturday. Paul Kane/Getty Images Since then, Fraser has led the Blues to 10 wins, two losses and a draw to secure them a wildcard finals berth. Although initially saying he didn’t want the senior coach role full-time, the hot run of form convinced Fraser he was ready, with the Blues officially appointing him on a three-year deal earlier this week.



Longmuir, who played 139 games for the Dockers as a ruck-forward, was thrilled to welcome Fraser – a former Suns and Magpies ruckman – into the coaching club. “He seems composed and process-orientated. He’s an ex-ruck as well, so he’s one for the clan,” Longmuir said ahead of Saturday’s clash with Carlton at Marvel Stadium. “There’s a few of us getting around now, which is nice to see. “He’s done a great job at not only instilling a lot of confidence in that team and belief, but bringing together a football team first and foremost, and then a club and a supporter base who’s got right behind them.” The Dockers (19-3) are already guaranteed to finish first, while 10th-placed Carlton (11-10-1) can only move up one spot.



Fremantle have rested Sam Switkowski, Jye Amiss and Heath Chapman for the match, bringing in small forward Tobyn Murray for his AFL debut, alongside Bailey Banfield and Judd McVee. Related Article Fremantle Dockers Your guide to the AFL finals in Fremantle as the Port City turns purple Carlton replaced injured duo Will Hayward and Nick Haynes with Lewis Young and Oliver Hollands. Fremantle are yet to win a flag in their 32-year history, with their closest effort coming in 2013 when they lost the grand final to Hawthorn by 15 points. The Dockers’ odds of winning this year’s premiership were given a further boost this week when second-placed Sydney suspended five players for the rest of the season, including stars Isaac Heeney, Chad Warner and Nick Blakey.



Fremantle are a perfect 12-0 at Optus Stadium this year, giving them a perfect runway to lock in a grand final berth, but Switkowski says the players aren’t thinking about the prospect of flag success just yet. “I think it’s pretty dangerous to let it wander that far,” Switkowski said. “There’s so much work to be done. It’s been a long time since we’ve even made it to a preliminary final. We haven’t been there year-on-year.” Switkowski described sealing the minor premiership as an “awesome achievement” for the club. “But clearly we’ve got bigger fish to fry, so that’s where our focus is going to be,” he said. AAP

World.title: Watch LIVE: Swans AFLW captain and coach speak for the first time amid club scandal
World.content:
Swans AFLW captain Lucy McEvoy and coach Colin O’Riordan are speaking for the first time since five of the club’s men’s players were stood down for breaching club standards, and a police investigation into an alleged sexual assault continues.

The Swans AFLW team are playing as part of a double-header at the SCG on Sunday. It will be just the second time the women’s team have played for competition points at the historic ground, but the occasion has been overshadowed by the sexual assault allegation surrounding members of the men’s team.

Loading

McEvoy and O’Riordan are speaking three hours after men’s team captain Callum Mills and coach Dean Cox broke their silence on the situation, with Mills apologising for the “actions of a few within our group”.

The five players – James Jordon, Chad Warner, Isaac Heeney, Riley Bice and Nick Blakey – along with an ex-AFL player and a mystery man were partying in a hotel room in Melbourne’s east in the early hours of Monday morning when the alleged assault took place.

World.title: Police code word at centre of tragic Lily Hooper bungle
World.content:
The miscommunication of a radio code word, set by NSW Police to signal missing bushwalker Lily Hooper had been found, is being blamed for an officer mistakenly telling the 18-year-old’s distraught family she had survived after eight days missing in the state’s Southern Highlands. Hooper’s body was on Thursday night retrieved from dense bush in the Nattai National Park, about 120 kilometres south-west of Sydney, where she had been missing since August 12. Hooper was last seen leaving her Oakdale home in Sydney’s south-west that morning, after telling family she was going hiking. Friends, family and loved ones of Sydney bushwalker Lily Hooper have been grieving her loss, having initially heard she was found alive. A multi-agency investigation has been launched to examine a series of failures that left Hooper’s parents, Jim and Kirrily Hooper, believing for almost 20 minutes that their daughter had been found alive, and celebrating with loved ones and media gathered at the search base on the edge of the national park. A police officer relayed the apparent good news to the Hooper family after an SES search party found the 18-year-old around 11.30am on Thursday. About 20 minutes later they were informed the teenager was dead.



Facing questions about the bungle on Friday, NSW State Emergency Service Commissioner Mike Wassing said NSW Police, which was leading the multi-agency search for Hooper, had set the code word and briefed search parties on it. Neither agency has confirmed the code word, citing the ongoing investigation. The miscommunication may have been sparked by a radio code believed to be used by SES searchers to report that a body has been found, in which they refer to full, half or empty water bottles to signal whether a person is alive, in the event family members may be monitoring the radio. A half bottle of water is believed to indicate a person’s condition is unclear. Lily’s father Jim, wearing an orange high-vis jacket, is embraced at the command post on Thursday. Kate Geraghty “It’s quite common that during search-and-rescue operations, police will set a code for the search-and-rescue operators to use with respect to if they find the missing person,” Wassing said. “In this case, there was a code that was applied. We’re working currently with police with respect to any of the misinformation associated with that code or any subsequent further information or communication.”



Wassing said investigators were focused on identifying how the miscommunication occurred and preventing a repeat, rather than blaming a particular agency or its officers. Whether the SES crew that found Hooper relayed incorrect information to the search base would form part of the agency’s investigation, he said. NSW State Emergency Service Commissioner Mike Wassing on Friday. KATE GERAGHTY Authorities say the relaying of the correct information to Hooper’s family was probably delayed by poor radio signal, which is also being investigated as potentially contributing to the initial miscommunication. The use of radio codes during missing-persons searches was being reviewed as part of the SES’ investigation into Thursday’s events, Wassing said. NSW Police Commissioner Mal Lanyon was forced to apologise for the miscommunication.



Facing a second day of scrutiny, Lanyon said the miscommunication was not born of ill will but elation that Hooper had been found. Police sought to correct the information at the earliest opportunity. “Tragically, her condition was miscommunicated, and for that I apologise,” he said. NSW Police Commissioner Mal Lanyon has apologised to the Hooper family for the miscommunication. KATE GERAGHTY Emergency Services Minister Jihad Dib said the state government would work with the SES and NSW Police to gather details around the search-and-rescue operation broadly, and the miscommunication. “This is not about an issue of looking [at] who’s to blame, this is about an issue of working out what it was that happened,” he said.



Related Article Tragedy How a family, police and politicians were wrongly told about bushwalker’s survival NSW Premier Chris Minns was forced to apologise to a budget estimates committee after incorrectly announcing that Hooper had been found alive. “The government, myself, we’re profoundly sorry,” Minns said on Friday. Minns said he hoped to speak with the Hooper family personally in the coming days. The information was passed from police to the premier via Police Minister Yasmin Catley. Lanyon said this was not unusual for a high-profile investigation.



Almost 1000 searchers from the Australian Defence Force, NSW SES and the Rural Fire Service had scoured dense bush in the national park alongside police looking for Hooper since she was reported missing. Hooper’s Hyundai was found near the start of the Bonnum Pic walking trail, a challenging 16-kilometre hike, shortly after she was reported missing. World.title: Cruise lines are relying on cutting-edge technology to clean up their acts
World.content:
Travel newsCruises Cruise lines are relying on cutting-edge technology to clean up their acts Brian Johnston August 21, 2026 — 1:07pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The cruise industry has a poor environmental record, has been regularly fined for flouting environmental regulations, and produces opaque and selective environmental reporting. On the other hand, cruise lines are making changes, and none are more ambitious than those that address how ships are fuelled. Biofuels, lower-emission fuels and less-polluting onshore power supply while in port are high on the agenda. An artist’s impression of Hurtigruten’s Sea Zero project, which aims to use battery power as its main energy source. Statistics from the Cruise Lines International Association (CLIA), which represents most of the world’s cruise lines, show slow progress in the right direction. In 2018, only one cruise ship had dual-fuel capacity while 55 had the technology to use onshore power. In 2025, that was up to 23 and 166 ships, respectively. CLIA represents 310 ships in total.



For a while, cruise lines touted their use of liquid natural gas (LNG) as a fuel. That was a positive move, since LNG is the most eco-friendly marine fuel available. But it does remain a fossil-fuel pollutant. 



Another inventive company worth watching is Ponant, which in early 2024 became the first ocean cruise line to be awarded official Green Globe Certification, recognised by the Global Sustainable Tourism Council. Ponant is fitting its fleet with systems to reduce nitrogen-oxide emissions. Ponant had previously abandoned heavy fuel and is now completing the fitting of its fleet with shore-power connection systems and catalytic systems to reduce nitrogen-oxide emissions. The company is also involved in European projects to advance innovative low-carbon energy technologies, among them a sail power system and hull that aims to provide 50 per cent of required propulsion energy using wind power. Meanwhile, Viking’s newest ship, Viking Libra, the world’s first hydrogen-powered cruise ship, launches in Europe this November.



The propulsion system is only partially based on liquefied hydrogen and fuel cells, so it won’t be operating with zero emissions all the time, but it’s a step in the right direction. Viking Libra will be the company’s most environmentally friendly vessel, and another will follow in 2027. Viking Libra, seen here under construction, is celebrated as the world’s first hydrogen-powered cruise ship. Of course, there’s a long way to go. The world’s biggest cruise companies emit as much carbon annually as a city of 600,000 people. The latest infamous Cruise Ship Report Card produced by Friends of the Earth still fails some cruise lines on air-pollution reduction. Only two (Hurtigruten and HX) get higher than a C grade. Not exactly smooth sailing, then, but hopefully fairer winds ahead. PORT GUIDE



Naples sits on one of Europe’s most generous and beautiful bays. iStock This 2500-year-old Italian city attracts a poor reputation yet has dazzling architecture and art museums, and terrific street life and food. Who goes there Naples is typically visited by larger cruise ships from companies such as MSC, Princess and Royal Caribbean, while smaller more luxury ships tend to anchor off nearby Sorrento on the Amalfi Coast. But that’s no hard and fast rule: mid-sized ships from Cunard, Viking and the like, and luxury ships from Regent Seven Seas or Silversea may occasionally call in. They’re all usually sailing western Mediterranean cruises, or cruises along the French and Italian Rivieras. Sail on in Naples sits on one of Europe’s most generous and beautiful bays, which is backed by the volcanic cone of Mount Vesuvius and dotted with small, rugged islands. You should certainly ensure you’re on deck to see the spectacle. Closer to port, you’ll enjoy the sight of Naples rising from waterfront fortifications in a series of hillside palaces and churches, topped by a whopping fort. Washing hung off balconies is a common sight in Naples. iStock



Berth rites The Stazione Marittima at Molo Angioino is a large four-storey cruise terminal that incorporates a convention centre, shopping mall, souvenir shops, restaurants and cafes, ATM terminals and tourist information desks. A metro station is close by and the ferry pier (for places such as Sorrento or Capri) adjacent. The terminal is a short walk from the city centre and a 30-minute walk from the historical centre. Going ashore Naples has chaotic energy, lovely churches, outstanding museums and enormous dollops of dolce vita. If you can deal with pollution, traffic and dilapidation, you’ll fall under its spell. Among the city’s highlights are the Royal Palace with its absurd excesses, overlooking the city’s most beautiful square, Piazza del Plebiscito. Ceiling fresco in Chiesa di San Ferdinando, a 17th-century church in the heart of Naples, right across from the Royal Palace. iStock Medieval Castel Nuovo fronts Piazza Municipio. The cathedral and the San Gennaro Catacombs are also worth visiting. Then soak up the street life along the waterfront, shopping drag Via Chiaia and historical street Spaccanapoli, and in the tangled lanes of Quartieri Spagnoli district. Don’t miss The National Archaeological Museum isn’t the best-organised or the most vigorously dusted, but it does provide one of the world’s best ensembles of archaeological objects, including superb Greco-Roman treasures such as sculptures, frescoes, ceramics and mosaics (plus some startling erotica) from Pompeii and Herculaneum. The museum also has good Italian painting and Egyptian collections.



Get active If you rent an e-bike, you can cycle westwards around the Bay of Naples and in half an hour reach Posillipo, a wealthy district with superb views from its hills and waterfront parks and beaches. For something different, Baia Underwater Archaeological Park a half-hour’s drive west allows you to snorkel or dive amid submerged Roman remains, including statues and mosaics. Best bites Naples has some of the world’s best street food. Pizza was invented here, and the classic choice is a margherita or marinara. Two variations are pizza fritta (folded and deep-fried) and pizza a portafoglio (also folded, and modestly sized). Neapolitans have a fondness for deep-fried nibbles such as calamari, fish, zucchini flowers, arancini or croquettes served in paper cones. Graffe is the local doughnut served sprinkled with sugar. Sfogliatelle pastries are a highlight of a trip to Naples. iStock Further afield There are rich shore-excursion pickings around Naples, but you’ll want to study how much coach travel is involved before signing up. The most popular options are visits to ancient Roman sites Pompeii or Herculaneum, both destroyed during the eruption of Mount Vesuvius in AD79, or to Sorrento and the Amalfi Coast, which offer cliff-clinging towns and pure blue waters. The island of Capri is another favourite, with stunning scenery and a hodgepodge of Roman ruins, chic villages and sea grottoes. Related Article Europe Italy’s most chaotic city is finally getting the reboot it deserves



EVERYONE ASKS Do cruise lines have seniors’ rates? Some occasionally do, but look carefully at the fare because your deal might be no better – or might even be worse – than other types of deals regularly offered by cruise lines. MSC Cruises, for example, offers up to 10 per cent off for those over 65. Celebrity Cruises offers discounts for those over 55, but how much depends on the specific sailing and only applies to a certain number of cabins. Most big budget ships offer some form of discount to seniors, usually those over 55. However, they’re often offered at the last minute (two months or less before the sail date) because cruise lines know seniors who aren’t working are free to hop on board at short notice.



Some might offer savings of no more than $100. You’d have to balance that against higher last-minute airfares or hotel bookings. Anyway, last-minute deals are hard to book on Australian cruises, where cabin capacity is tight. Still, all other things being equal, $100 or any other discount is better than a poke in the eye, as my grandfather used to say, so no harm in asking at the time of booking. If booking direct online, some cruise lines have a filter or deals tab from which you can select the seniors option. World.title: One-pan creamy mushroom, kale and Dijon mustard risoni
World.content:
Step 1 Warm a wide saute pan over high heat. Add the olive oil, mushrooms and ¼ cup of water with a good pinch of salt. Cook until the mushrooms have released all their liquid and it has evaporated, allowing the mushrooms to start to brown.

Step 2 Add the onion and cavolo nero and saute together for about 3-4 minutes until the onions have turned translucent.

Step 3 Stir in the risoni, stock and cream with another good pinch of salt and some black pepper. Bring to a low simmer and adjust the heat so it stays at a gentle simmer.

Step 4 Cover the pan with a tight-fitting lid and cook on low for 10-12 minutes, removing the lid to stir the risoni every couple of minutes until it is al dente. You may need to occasionally add a splash of water to maintain a risotto-like

consistency.

Step 5 Turn off the heat and stir in the lemon juice, Dijon mustard and grated parmigiano reggiano. Season to taste.

World.title: Accused rapist identified, police say he went to work then returned to scene
World.content:
A man accused of raping a young woman on her early-morning walk went to work after the alleged assault before returning to the scene that evening, according to police. Jacob Dave Henry Hauraki, 32, allegedly assaulted the woman in bushes near Moggill Creek in Brookfield, a semi-rural suburb west of Brisbane, after approaching her from behind along Brookfield Road about 6.33am on Thursday. The 23-year-old fought him off, crossing a nearby creek and traversing bushland into Brookfield Showgrounds to escape before calling Triple Zero. There was a heavy police presence in Brookfield on Thursday. NINE “I want to acknowledge the victim this morning and recognise her bravery,” Detective Superintendent Andrew Massingham told reporters on Friday morning.



“This is a horrific and confronting incident that no one should ever experience.” The woman had been on a walk with a family member, who had ended up separated. She was injured in the alleged attack and taken to the Royal Brisbane and Women’s Hospital, but had returned home by Friday. Massingham said police made a breakthrough on Thursday evening, after witnesses came forward with dashcam footage. They allege Hauraki was on his way to work in another location when he attacked the woman, who he did not know.



He then went on to work about 15 minutes away but returned that evening to the scene, and police recognised his vehicle and made an arrest on Moons Lane. “We’re fairly familiar with offenders sometimes returning to the scene for different reasons,” Massingham said. Detective superintendent Andrew Massingham speaking on the alleged assault at police headquarters in Brisbane on Friday morning. William Davis Hauraki was charged with six counts of rape, stalking, assault with intent to commit rape, assault occasioning bodily harm and deprivation of liberty. Massingham said the crime scene would remain in place, with police divers searching the creek.



“We’d obviously be very keen on trying to identify any further items that the offender may have dropped or left behind in our forensic search.” An investigation command centre had been established in Ferny Grove, with a mobile beat set up at the showgrounds. Nine News The man did not appear for his mention in Brisbane’s Magistrate Court on Friday, or apply for bail. The matter was adjourned until September 18. World.content:
Plymouth Brethren Christian Church spokesman and elder Lloyd Grimshaw is doing a very specific thing at the parliamentary inquiry into interference at the 2025 federal election: he’s trying to say that the mass participation in the election campaign was all about individual church members acting voluntarily, not the church itself.



So member for Kooyong Monique Ryan asks him specifically, and quotes his “Man of God” Bruce Hales to do so: “Among the writings of Mr Hales is a statement that says that everything you do in your daily life is church business. That being the case, there’s a certain inconsistency here?”

Loading

The quote she’s referring to is one from 2014, when Hales said: “Assembly-minded persons would carry the feature of the house of God everywhere we go. So wherever we are, in any circumstance, in every detail of our lives, we’d be related to the house of God”.



Grimshaw says this should be read in context, “that you know, it’s in your daily life, the church members’ daily life, they’re observed as being part of the Christian faith, and they should act accordingly. So they should act in accord with their Christian faith.”



Following today’s reports about the far-right, Ryan is going through the far-right stunts one by one that she personally was subjected to during the 2025 election campaign and asking Grimshaw to answer whether he knew of any of these people.



“I’d like to ask … whether the brethren has any relationship with or has funded in any way a former member of the Proud Boys by the name of Harrison McLean, who interrupted an asylum seeker resource centre event on the 23rd of April?”

Members of the Plymouth Brethren Christian Church in Tasmania in 2025.

“It’s the first time I’ve ever heard the name,” he says. McLean has declined to comment to this masthead about his electoral activity.



What about agitator Matt Trihey, she asks – who conducted a stunt in Kooyong? Neo-Nazi Joel Davis? No and no, Grimshaw answers.



She’s also asked about the payments, reported in this masthead this morning, to right-wing agitators to run stunts. Again, Grimshaw dead-bats it using the familiar argument.



“The Brethren, Plymouth Brethren Christian Church never funded one cent to any political cause or party or candidate in the 2025 election.”

World.title: Young Docker set for AFL debut as Freo rest three for Blues clash
World.content:
NationalWAAFL 2026 Young Docker set for AFL debut as Freo rest three for Blues clash Justin Chadwick August 21, 2026 — 1:42pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Fremantle coach Justin Longmuir has welcomed Josh Fraser to his special ruck club, praising the new Carlton coach for the way he’s turned around the Blues’ fortunes. Carlton were a rabble at 1-8 when Fraser inherited the coaching reins on an interim basis following Michael Voss’ decision to step down. Tobyn Murray is set to make his AFL debut when Fremantle take on Carlton on Saturday. Paul Kane/Getty Images Since then, Fraser has led the Blues to 10 wins, two losses and a draw to secure them a wildcard finals berth. Although initially saying he didn’t want the senior coach role full-time, the hot run of form convinced Fraser he was ready, with the Blues officially appointing him on a three-year deal earlier this week.



Longmuir, who played 139 games for the Dockers as a ruck-forward, was thrilled to welcome Fraser – a former Suns and Magpies ruckman – into the coaching club. “He seems composed and process-orientated. He’s an ex-ruck as well, so he’s one for the clan,” Longmuir said ahead of Saturday’s clash with Carlton at Marvel Stadium. “There’s a few of us getting around now, which is nice to see. “He’s done a great job at not only instilling a lot of confidence in that team and belief, but bringing together a football team first and foremost, and then a club and a supporter base who’s got right behind them.” The Dockers (19-3) are already guaranteed to finish first, while 10th-placed Carlton (11-10-1) can only move up one spot.



Fremantle have rested Sam Switkowski, Jye Amiss and Heath Chapman for the match, bringing in small forward Tobyn Murray for his AFL debut, alongside Bailey Banfield and Judd McVee. Related Article Fremantle Dockers Your guide to the AFL finals in Fremantle as the Port City turns purple Carlton replaced injured duo Will Hayward and Nick Haynes with Lewis Young and Oliver Hollands. Fremantle are yet to win a flag in their 32-year history, with their closest effort coming in 2013 when they lost the grand final to Hawthorn by 15 points. The Dockers’ odds of winning this year’s premiership were given a further boost this week when second-placed Sydney suspended five players for the rest of the season, including stars Isaac Heeney, Chad Warner and Nick Blakey.



Fremantle are a perfect 12-0 at Optus Stadium this year, giving them a perfect runway to lock in a grand final berth, but Switkowski says the players aren’t thinking about the prospect of flag success just yet. “I think it’s pretty dangerous to let it wander that far,” Switkowski said. “There’s so much work to be done. It’s been a long time since we’ve even made it to a preliminary final. We haven’t been there year-on-year.” Switkowski described sealing the minor premiership as an “awesome achievement” for the club. “But clearly we’ve got bigger fish to fry, so that’s where our focus is going to be,” he said. World.title: Police code word at centre of tragic Lily Hooper bungle
World.content:
The miscommunication of a radio code word, set by NSW Police to signal missing bushwalker Lily Hooper had been found, is being blamed for an officer mistakenly telling the 18-year-old’s distraught family she had survived after eight days missing in the state’s Southern Highlands. Hooper’s body was on Thursday night retrieved from dense bush in the Nattai National Park, about 120 kilometres south-west of Sydney, where she had been missing since August 12. Hooper was last seen leaving her Oakdale home in Sydney’s south-west that morning, after telling family she was going hiking. Friends, family and loved ones of Sydney bushwalker Lily Hooper have been grieving her loss, having initially heard she was found alive. A multi-agency investigation has been launched to examine a series of failures that left Hooper’s parents, Jim and Kirrily Hooper, believing for almost 20 minutes that their daughter had been found alive, and celebrating with loved ones and media gathered at the search base on the edge of the national park. A police officer relayed the apparent good news to the Hooper family after an SES search party found the 18-year-old around 11.30am on Thursday. About 20 minutes later they were informed the teenager was dead.



Facing questions about the bungle on Friday, NSW State Emergency Service Commissioner Mike Wassing said NSW Police, which was leading the multi-agency search for Hooper, had set the code word and briefed search parties on it. Neither agency has confirmed the code word, citing the ongoing investigation. The miscommunication may have been sparked by a radio code believed to be used by SES searchers to report that a body has been found, in which they refer to full, half or empty water bottles to signal whether a person is alive, in the event family members may be monitoring the radio. A half bottle of water is believed to indicate a person’s condition is unclear. Lily’s father Jim, wearing an orange high-vis jacket, is embraced at the command post on Thursday. Kate Geraghty “It’s quite common that during search-and-rescue operations, police will set a code for the search-and-rescue operators to use with respect to if they find the missing person,” Wassing said. “In this case, there was a code that was applied. We’re working currently with police with respect to any of the misinformation associated with that code or any subsequent further information or communication.”



Wassing said investigators were focused on identifying how the miscommunication occurred and preventing a repeat, rather than blaming a particular agency or its officers. Whether the SES crew that found Hooper relayed incorrect information to the search base would form part of the agency’s investigation, he said. NSW State Emergency Service Commissioner Mike Wassing on Friday. KATE GERAGHTY Authorities say the relaying of the correct information to Hooper’s family was probably delayed by poor radio signal, which is also being investigated as potentially contributing to the initial miscommunication. The use of radio codes during missing-persons searches was being reviewed as part of the SES’ investigation into Thursday’s events, Wassing said. NSW Police Commissioner Mal Lanyon was forced to apologise for the miscommunication.



Facing a second day of scrutiny, Lanyon said the miscommunication was not born of ill will but elation that Hooper had been found. Police sought to correct the information at the earliest opportunity. “Tragically, her condition was miscommunicated, and for that I apologise,” he said. NSW Police Commissioner Mal Lanyon has apologised to the Hooper family for the miscommunication. KATE GERAGHTY Emergency Services Minister Jihad Dib said the state government would work with the SES and NSW Police to gather details around the search-and-rescue operation broadly, and the miscommunication. “This is not about an issue of looking [at] who’s to blame, this is about an issue of working out what it was that happened,” he said.



Related Article Tragedy How a family, police and politicians were wrongly told about bushwalker’s survival NSW Premier Chris Minns was forced to apologise to a budget estimates committee after incorrectly announcing that Hooper had been found alive. “The government, myself, we’re profoundly sorry,” Minns said on Friday. Minns said he hoped to speak with the Hooper family personally in the coming days. The information was passed from police to the premier via Police Minister Yasmin Catley. Lanyon said this was not unusual for a high-profile investigation.



Almost 1000 searchers from the Australian Defence Force, NSW SES and the Rural Fire Service had scoured dense bush in the national park alongside police looking for Hooper since she was reported missing. Hooper’s Hyundai was found near the start of the Bonnum Pic walking trail, a challenging 16-kilometre hike, shortly after she was reported missing. Lily Hooper began her hike on the Bonnum Pic Walking Trail on August 12. Kate Geraghty Wollondilly Shire Mayor Matt Gould, whose electorate encompasses Nattai National Park, said flags on the council chambers would be flown at half-mast. “They are small gestures but I hope they help show in some way just how deeply Lily’s loss is being felt across our community, and how much Wollondilly is thinking of her family, friends and everyone who loved her,” he wrote on social media.



Bujutsu Martial Arts and Fitness Centre, where Hooper had trained in Muay Thai and Brazilian ju-jitsu for the past two years, also paid tribute. She was months away from receiving her blue belt in Brazilian ju-jitsu. “She was a talented and tough martial artist, but despite that toughness, Lily was such a lovely person. She was one of those people who everyone simply liked,” Sensei Mark Szalajko wrote on social media. The most popular options are visits to ancient Roman sites Pompeii or Herculaneum, both destroyed during the eruption of Mount Vesuvius in AD79, or to Sorrento and the Amalfi Coast, which offer cliff-clinging towns and pure blue waters. The island of Capri is another favourite, with stunning scenery and a hodgepodge of Roman ruins, chic villages and sea grottoes. Related Article Europe Italy’s most chaotic city is finally getting the reboot it deserves



EVERYONE ASKS Do cruise lines have seniors’ rates? Some occasionally do, but look carefully at the fare because your deal might be no better – or might even be worse – than other types of deals regularly offered by cruise lines. MSC Cruises, for example, offers up to 10 per cent off for those over 65. Celebrity Cruises offers discounts for those over 55, but how much depends on the specific sailing and only applies to a certain number of cabins. Most big budget ships offer some form of discount to seniors, usually those over 55. However, they’re often offered at the last minute (two months or less before the sail date) because cruise lines know seniors who aren’t working are free to hop on board at short notice.



Some might offer savings of no more than $100. You’d have to balance that against higher last-minute airfares or hotel bookings. Anyway, last-minute deals are hard to book on Australian cruises, where cabin capacity is tight. Still, all other things being equal, $100 or any other discount is better than a poke in the eye, as my grandfather used to say, so no harm in asking at the time of booking. If booking direct online, some cruise lines have a filter or deals tab from which you can select the seniors option. World.title: One-pan creamy mushroom, kale and Dijon mustard risoni
World.content:
Step 1 Warm a wide saute pan over high heat. Add the olive oil, mushrooms and ¼ cup of water with a good pinch of salt. Cook until the mushrooms have released all their liquid and it has evaporated, allowing the mushrooms to start to brown.

Step 2 Add the onion and cavolo nero and saute together for about 3-4 minutes until the onions have turned translucent.

Step 3 Stir in the risoni, stock and cream with another good pinch of salt and some black pepper. Bring to a low simmer and adjust the heat so it stays at a gentle simmer.

Step 4 Cover the pan with a tight-fitting lid and cook on low for 10-12 minutes, removing the lid to stir the risoni every couple of minutes until it is al dente. You may need to occasionally add a splash of water to maintain a risotto-like

consistency.

Step 5 Turn off the heat and stir in the lemon juice, Dijon mustard and grated parmigiano reggiano. Season to taste.

World.title: Accused rapist identified, police say he went to work then returned to scene
World.content:
A man accused of raping a young woman on her early-morning walk went to work after the alleged assault before returning to the scene that evening, according to police. Jacob Dave Henry Hauraki, 32, allegedly assaulted the woman in bushes near Moggill Creek in Brookfield, a semi-rural suburb west of Brisbane, after approaching her from behind along Brookfield Road about 6.33am on Thursday. The 23-year-old fought him off, crossing a nearby creek and traversing bushland into Brookfield Showgrounds to escape before calling Triple Zero. There was a heavy police presence in Brookfield on Thursday. NINE “I want to acknowledge the victim this morning and recognise her bravery,” Detective Superintendent Andrew Massingham told reporters on Friday morning.



“This is a horrific and confronting incident that no one should ever experience.” The woman had been on a walk with a family member, who had ended up separated. She was injured in the alleged attack and taken to the Royal Brisbane and Women’s Hospital, but had returned home by Friday. Massingham said police made a breakthrough on Thursday evening, after witnesses came forward with dashcam footage. They allege Hauraki was on his way to work in another location when he attacked the woman, who he did not know.



He then went on to work about 15 minutes away but returned that evening to the scene, and police recognised his vehicle and made an arrest on Moons Lane. “We’re fairly familiar with offenders sometimes returning to the scene for different reasons,” Massingham said. Detective superintendent Andrew Massingham speaking on the alleged assault at police headquarters in Brisbane on Friday morning. William Davis Hauraki was charged with six counts of rape, stalking, assault with intent to commit rape, assault occasioning bodily harm and deprivation of liberty. Massingham said the crime scene would remain in place, with police divers searching the creek.



“We’d obviously be very keen on trying to identify any further items that the offender may have dropped or left behind in our forensic search.” An investigation command centre had been established in Ferny Grove, with a mobile beat set up at the showgrounds. Nine News The man did not appear for his mention in Brisbane’s Magistrate Court on Friday, or apply for bail. The matter was adjourned until September 18.
